title: すずらん三十万部  (Suzuran Sells Three Hundred Thousand)

segments.t: At Hokudai Kanda's bookstore counter, eager customers crowd around manager Tayama asking for the new edition titled Suzuran at fifteen thousand yen a copy. Meanwhile in his quiet garden, Poseidon boss Ikezawa hears that Suzuran has already sold three hundred thousand copies. Just soak in the shop-counter rhythm first.
「すずらん」ください。
一万五千円です。
ありがとうございました。
僕も「すずらん」。
「すずらん」お願いします。
ありがとうございます。
派手にいったもんだな。
すでに三十万部ほど売り上げてるのか。
自由をはき違えたかな。
分かった、今行くから。
思いどおりにはいかないもんだ。
You just heard a textbook Japanese shop transaction followed by Ikezawa's dry reflection. Let's look closer at each line.
「すずらん」ください。
'Suzuran, please.' Naming an item and adding "kudasai" is the simplest way in Japanese to ask for something over a counter, whether a book, a ticket, or a cup of coffee.
一万五千円です。
'That is fifteen thousand yen.' Counting in units of "man"—ten thousand—makes fifteen thousand "ichiman gosen", one ten-thousand plus five thousand, followed by "en" for yen.
ありがとうございました。
'Thank you very much.' Shop staff say "arigatou gozaimashita" with "mashita" at the end once a sale wraps up, thanking you for a transaction that is now complete.
僕も「すずらん」。
'Suzuran for me too.' "Boku" is a warm, polite-casual word for 'I' used mostly by men and boys. Adding "mo", too or also, turns "boku mo" into an easy 'me too!'.
「すずらん」お願いします。
'Suzuran, please.' Alongside "kudasai", "onegaishimasu" is the other counter classic for ordering—slightly softer, literally entrusting your request to the clerk.
ありがとうございます。
'Thank you very much.' Compare "arigatou gozaimasu" here with "gozaimashita" a moment ago: while cash is still changing hands, the clerk stays in the present form.
派手にいったもんだな。
'He really went big with this.' "Hade ni" means flashily or on a grand scale, from "hade", flashy. Ending on "itta mon da na" voices rueful admiration at how far Muranishi pushed things.
すでに三十万部ほど売り上げてるのか。

'He has already sold around three hundred thousand copies, huh.' "Sudeni" means already, while "sanjuuman-bu" pairs thirty "man"—three hundred thousand—with "bu", the counter for printed copies, plus "hodo" for 'approximately'.
分かった、今行くから。

'Got it, I am coming right now.' "Wakatta" is casual 'got it' or 'understood', and "ima iku kara"—literally 'because I am going now'—is how Japanese speakers call back 'coming right now!' whereas English says 'I am coming'.
思いどおりにはいかないもんだ。

'Things never go the way you expect.' "Omoidoori" welds "omoi", thought or wish, to "doori", just as, while "ikanai mon da" sighs that life rarely goes according to plan. Now let's listen to the whole bookstore and garden scene again without pauses.
「すずらん」ください。
一万五千円です。
ありがとうございました。
僕も「すずらん」。
「すずらん」お願いします。
ありがとうございます。
派手にいったもんだな。
すでに三十万部ほど売り上げてるのか。
自由をはき違えたかな。
分かった、今行くから。
思いどおりにはいかないもんだ。
With "kudasai", "onegaishimasu", and "boku mo", you can already step up to any counter in Japan, and counting by "man" unlocks big yen prices right away. See you again.
また会いましょう。
